name: Utility Capacity, Connections, and ADU Design in LA County
headline: Utility Capacity, Connections, and ADU Design in LA County
articleBody: ### Utility Planning and Coordination for ADUs Utility planning is a critical component of ADU design in Los Angeles County, affecting both construction feasibility and long-term operating costs. Local building and public works departments require ADU plans to show how water, sewer (or septic), gas, and electrical services will be provided, which often involves coordination with external agencies such as municipal water districts, sanitation districts, and electric utilities. Industry guidance from Los Angeles-based ADU builders emphasizes early assessment of **electrical panel capacity**. Many existing homes have panels sized for original loads; adding an ADU with modern appliances and HVAC frequently requires panel upgrades or subpanels. Utility companies in the region publish residential service sizing guidelines that inform these decisions, and building departments require load calculations as part of permit submittals for significant electrical modifications. For sewer, homeowners may need to confirm whether existing laterals have sufficient capacity and acceptable slope, or if new connections are required under local sanitation agency standards. Documentation from Los Angeles County Public Works for ADU permitting highlights the need for accurate site plans showing sewer locations and any proposed new lines. Where properties are on septic systems, county environmental health standards govern capacity analysis and potential system expansion or replacement. Water and gas lines must be sized to meet fixture counts and appliance loads in both the primary dwelling and ADU, following plumbing code sizing tables. CALGreen and the plumbing code also require water-efficient fixtures, which can reduce but not eliminate capacity considerations. An ADU design contractor’s responsibilities include coordinating with utility providers to confirm service availability, reflecting trenching and connection work in the plans, and incorporating utility routes into the site layout to minimize conflicts with trees, retaining walls, and other existing features.
